qs.q: A 65-year-old man with a history of chronic smoking and industrial dye exposure presents with gross hematuria and flank pain. Imaging reveals a filling defect within the renal pelvis. Histologic examination demonstrates malignant cells originating from transitional epithelium. What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Juxtaglomerular cell tumor of the cortex
Urothelial carcinoma of the renal pelvis
Squamous cell carcinoma of the calyx
Renal cell carcinoma with sarcomatoid change
qs.e: Urothelial carcinoma of the renal pelvis arises from the transitional cell lining, sharing risk factors and histologic features with bladder cancer. Renal cell carcinoma originates from the renal parenchyma rather than the transitional epithelium of the collecting system.
qs.s: Urinary Tract Obstruction & Hydronephrosis: Causes, Symptoms: MCQs

qs.q: During a micturating cystourethrogram (MCUG), how is a ureterocele distinguished from a normal bladder or other filling defects?
o: By visualization of an open urachus draining to the umbilicus
By prompt disappearance of contrast during the micturition phase
By complete absence of contrast in the entire renal pelvis
By seeing a cystic filling defect within the contrast-filled bladder
qs.e: During MCUG, if there is no abnormality the bladder is uniformly white with contrast, but in a ureterocele, you will see a filling defect corresponding to the cystic dilation of the distal ureter. It represents the fluid-filled sac projecting into the bladder.
